transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reed (Redwood SE), Lena Zhou (Zenith Head of Platform), Carlos Mendes (Zenith SRE), Priya Rao (Zenith ML)

Summary: Quick discovery on incident tolerance, how Redwood's routing/fallback layers work, and trade-offs between Hosted/Dedicated/Private for Zenith's regulated workloads. Agreed to run a canary in staging and exchange security artifacts.

00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um I'm Maya, I'll lead this chat, Jonah's our solutions engineer, we're here to understand your incident tolerance goals and constraints, just super quick - is the agenda ok?
00:10 Lena (Zenith): yep that's fine, thanks, we'll mostly try to map our SLAs to what you provide and see how fallbacks would behave under degraded networks, we run across eu-west and us-central, some latency sensitive endpoints in us-central for our billing flows
00:25 Carlos (Zenith): and hi, we have strict audit and egress rules - so private deployment is on the table but we need to see trade-offs re: failover.
00:35 Jonah (Redwood SE): totally, thanks. Quick question: are you expecting active-active across regions or prefer active-primary with read-fallback?
00:45 Priya (Zenith): for model serving we prefer active-active for inference, main reason is latency; but for cost reasons we could accept active-primary for some heavy-batch endpoints. Also need to preserve exact input privacy for PHI-ish data so private infra matters.
01:05 Maya: helpful. High level, Redwood supports: hosted (our multi-tenant API with global routing), dedicated (reserved pools in chosen regions), and private (VPC/air-gapped). Each has different behaviour for fallback orchestration - hosted will reroute to nearest healthy region or compatible model variant, dedicated can do cross-region failover if you reserve across regions, private is under your control but our control plane can still orchestrate if you allow peering.
01:30 Carlos: when you say "compatible model variant" what does that mean in practice?
01:35 Jonah: good question - e.g., you might have a quantized 4-bit variant for cost/throughput and a 16-bit variant for quality. Our runtime tags variants as "compat" if they accept same input schema and produce same structured output. During outages we can route traffic to a lower-fidelity variant and mark responses with a special header so clients can apply tolerance logic. It's opt-in.
02:05 Lena: ok that helps. How do you handle KV-cache and prefix caching across regions? We rely on cache priming for top-heavy prompt patterns.
02:20 Jonah: currently prefix/KV caches are local to the serving pool; in hosted we do cross-region replication only for warm pools and tiered priming. For dedicated/private you can configure warm replicas in other regions, or use our cross-region cache warmers in the control plane - there's a trade-off: replication cost vs warm-start latency. Also we have sticky routing when cache hit rate is critical.
03:00 Priya: When a region has intermittent packet loss, do you failover immediately or try retries first? Our tolerance to staleness is low for billing.
03:15 Jonah: default policy is conservative: short retries (exponential backoff) + circuit breaker that trips after X failures per second; if the circuit is open we route to fallback region or variant based on policy. All of this is configurable per-route. You can choose aggressive failover for latency-critical routes or prefer retries for consistency. We'll share the policy matrix.
03:55 Carlos: do circuit breaker openings cause token billing to switch? like, if we route to a cheaper quantized model, do we pay at the cheaper rate automatically? We need accurate accounting.
04:10 Maya: yes, billing follows the actual model/route used. Our console gives token-level cost breakdown and we can tag requests so chargebacks map to route/version. For dedicated contracts we can set predictable unit pricing, but fallbacks to hosted variant may bill at hosted rates unless you have cross-contract allowances.
04:40 Priya: that answers the cost part. Next, how do you ensure compliance logs for private deployments - we need full audit trails and KMS integration.
04:55 Maya: for private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and ship audit logs to your SIEM via secure forwarders; we store minimal runtime telemetry in the control plane, but you can opt for fully self-hosted control plane for air-gapped. We'll attach our private deployment checklist and a network diagram.
05:20 Lena: great. A scenario: one AZ in eu-west goes down for 30 minutes. What would Redwood recommend for trade-offs between graceful degradation or failing over to us-central? We worry about data residency plus latency hit.
05:40 Jonah: options: 1) Graceful degradation: limit model size/response tokens (degraded mode) within region so you keep requests local; 2) Region failover: route to us-central with higher latencies but maintain throughput; 3) Service split: route non-sensitive ops to failover region and keep sensitive ops local with queueing. We typically recommend a hybrid: keep PHI-bound requests local with queueing and route non-PHI to fallback region. We can tag policies at route-level.
06:25 Carlos: how does queueing affect SLOs? For billing flows we have 99.95% p95 latency target, we can't queue for minutes.
06:35 Jonah: queueing is best-effort and should be reserved for non-latency-critical paths. For billing flows you'd use active-active or reserve dedicated capacity in both regions. For 99.95% p95 you likely need redundant capacity or multi-region dedicated pools plus health checks and fast DNS/edge steering.
07:05 Priya: any built-in testing for failover? like simulated regional outage drills?
07:12 Maya: yes, Redwood supports chaos drills via staged canary and failure injection: we can simulate region-level latency and traffic shaping in a sandbox, and we'll produce a postmortem template and a runbook.
07:30 Lena: can you share an example runbook?
07:33 Jonah: we'll drop a link - Link: https://redwood-internal.demo/runbooks/failover-sample (note: placeholder). It includes steps: identify degraded pool, open circuit breakers to avoid cascading failures, fail traffic to warm replica, monitor errors and rollback.
08:05 Carlos: on DNS vs control-plane steering - which is faster for you? We currently use weighted DNS with health checks and it's slow to converge.
08:20 Jonah: control-plane steering (our edge + smart routing) is faster and supports connection draining so in-flight requests are completed. DNS is coarser-grained and heavier TTL-limited. For sub-second reaction you want our edge routing. For private deployments we can provide an edge proxy in your VPC that listens to control-plane signals.
09:00 Priya: latency numbers - what's typical cross-region failover p95 added latency?
09:10 Jonah: depends on geography. From eu-west to us-central we see ballpark +120-250ms p95 for inference depending on model size; quantized smaller models skew lower. We'll run a bespoke profile against your traffic.
09:30 Maya: another practical point: feature parity for API behaviour during fallbacks. We return a response header x-redwood-fallback: region=us-central; variant=quant4; reason=circuit_open. Your client can detect that and apply UI fallbacks or escalate. We also support structured error payloads for programmatic flows.
10:05 Lena: ok that header is useful. On data residency - if we route to us-central as fallback are we able to redact or strip PII automatically?
10:20 Jonah: you can attach pre-processing hooks in the edge layer to scrub tokens or replace with surrogate IDs before routing to a non-resident region. That's part of private deployment weaving or can be a transform in the client SDK.
10:45 Carlos: SLA language - what uptime and latency SLOs are you comfortable committing to on Dedicated vs Hosted?
10:55 Maya: Hosted: multi-region customers often see>99.9% platform availability, but we only SLA 99.5% for standard hosted tiers. Dedicated: we can provide SLA gates up to 99.95% depending on commitment. For Private (self-managed) SLA is tied to the on-prem contract; Redwood's support SLAs can be layered. We'll have legal ops craft a section for the contract.
11:25 Priya: curious about fail-open vs fail-closed model for safety: does Redwood support enforcing model gating if a lower fidelity variant is used? We prefer fail-closed for certain workflows.
11:40 Jonah: yes, policies are per-route: fail-closed (reject), fail-open (route to variant), degrade-with-warning (route and tag) are all supported. You pick per-route.
12:00 Maya: quick alignment on timeline - you mentioned an internal pilot next month?
12:08 Lena: yes we'd like a 2-week pilot in staging with 10% canary traffic then ramp. Need your runbook and pricing breakdown to sign off.
12:20 Maya: great, we'll send the artifacts and set up the pilot calendar.
12:30 Carlos: last Q - for audit purposes can we get request/response hashes so we can prove non-repudiation?
12:38 Jonah: we provide per-request metadata and cryptographic request id and signed logs in private deployments; for hosted we provide detailed telemetry and can integrate with your SIEM - full signed logs require private or dedicated with log shipping enabled.
12:58 Maya: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up. Recap: send SOC2 + private checklist, runbook, cost model, schedule pilot.
13:15 Lena: thanks, looking forward to the docs.

Notes: transcription occasionally mislabels speakers and drops punctuation; some product names might be slightly off in the transcript (e.g., "quant4" shorthand). Shared artifacts referenced during call: Security packet (https://redwood.com/security/soc2.pdf), Pilot runbook (shared after call), Canary playbook (S3 link to be shared).

End of transcript.
